prompt: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of an application.
answer: So I think we did some performance work. Maybe the page was a bit slow and we tried some things like lazy loading and stuff. I think it got better after that. It was a team effort and everyone helped out. Generally I would say performance is important and we tried to keep an eye on it during the project overall.
note: no situation, no numbers, all 'we', heavy hedging

prompt: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of an application.
answer: On a client dashboard the initial load felt slow, so I profiled it with Lighthouse and found the main bundle was pulling in a charting library on every route. I split that out and lazy loaded it behind the route that actually used it, then memoised a list component that was re-rendering on every keystroke. Load time improved noticeably and the team kept the pattern for later routes.
note: clear actions and ownership, but no measured result

prompt: Tell me about a time you improved the performance of an application.
answer: On a client dashboard our LCP was 4.1 seconds and users were complaining the page felt broken on first load. I owned the fix. I profiled with Lighthouse and found two causes: the main bundle included a charting library used on one route, and a list component re-rendered on every keystroke. I code split the chart behind a lazy route, deferred the analytics script, and memoised the list rows. LCP came down to 1.9 seconds, measured in Lighthouse and confirmed in field data over the following two weeks. We added a bundle size budget in CI so it would not regress.
note: full STAR, owned, measured, and the result stuck

prompt: Tell me about a conflict you had with a teammate.
answer: Well there are always conflicts in teams right, I mean people disagree about things all the time. I remember there were a few situations where we did not agree about how to do something, maybe about the architecture or the approach, and usually what happens is you talk about it and then you find some compromise. I think communication is the most important thing honestly. In general I try to be diplomatic and not make it personal because at the end of the day we all want the project to succeed and that is what matters most for everyone involved.

prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision.
answer: The team wanted to put the transcription job in the same service as the API. I argued that a two hour call would block request handlers and that we would not be able to scale them independently, so I proposed pulling it into a separate worker consuming from a queue. I wrote up the two options with the tradeoffs and we discussed it in a design review.
note: concrete and well owned, but stops before the outcome

prompt: Tell me about a time you made a mistake in production.
answer: I shipped a Paddle webhook handler that was not idempotent. Paddle retries on timeout, so a slow database write meant one customer got charged credit twice within a minute. I found it the next morning in Sentry, added a unique constraint on the event id and made the handler upsert instead of insert, then backfilled the duplicate rows and refunded the customer. After that I made idempotency a checklist item for every webhook we integrate. It took about three hours from alert to fix.
note: specific, owned, measurable, includes the systemic follow-up
